docs.title: SparkVerse
docs.text:
A Hybrid Hardware-in-the-Loop Simulator for Multi-Robot Coordination

SparkVerse is a Unity-based simulation and visualisation platform that bridges physical robots with virtual digital twins over MQTT. It provides a real-time bird's-eye view of an arena, tracks physical robots, and lets you control the entire fleet through MQTT commands.

The platform supports two physical robot variants:

Variant Robots Localisation Location SparkVerse SparkNodes (custom 2WD) Overhead camera + OpenCV Monash University, Australia TurtleVerse TurtleBot3 Burger (ROS2) Qualisys motion capture IIT Bombay, India

Both variants share the same MQTT-based architecture and Unity digital-twin engine.

docs.title: Running the Simulation
docs.text: This guide assumes you've completed all three installation steps. You'll need three terminal windows plus the Unity editor.

docs.title: Step 1 — Start the MQTT Broker
docs.text:
Open a terminal and start Mosquitto:

/opt/homebrew/opt/mosquitto/sbin/mosquitto -c /opt/homebrew/etc/mosquitto/mosquitto.conf

Or, if you set it up as a background service:

brew services start mosquitto

Keep the broker running

The MQTT broker must stay running for the entire session. Everything — Unity, the camera script, your control commands — communicates through it.

docs.title: Step 2 — Start the Camera Detection Script (Optional)
docs.text:
If you have physical robots to track with an overhead camera, open a new terminal:

cd MAPF_sparkbug
python3 robot_traj_http.py

This launches the vision pipeline and a local HTTP server on port 8000 that Unity polls for real robot positions.

No physical robots?

If you're running a simulation-only session (no camera, no physical robots), you can skip this step entirely. The Unity sim works standalone with virtual robots.

docs.title: Step 3 — Prepare the Robot Configuration File
docs.text: Create a JSON file that defines the robots and arena layout. This file tells Unity how many robots to spawn and where to place them.

docs.title: JSON Structure Reference
docs.text:
Per-robot fields:

Field Type Description id int Unique robot identifier (convention: ≥ 1000) name string Display name (for debugging) x float X position in world space (metres) z float Z position in world space (metres)

Arena fields:

Field Type Description sizeX float Arena width (metres) sizeZ float Arena depth (metres) originX/Y/Z float Centre point of the arena

Copy the file path

You'll need the full file path of this JSON file in the next step. Select the file in Finder and press Option+Cmd+C to copy its path to the clipboard.

docs.title: Step 4 — Launch the Unity Simulation
docs.text:
1. Open the SparkVerse project in Unity (if not already open)
  2. Press the Play button (▶) at the top of the editor

Once the simulation starts, you'll be prompted to configure it:

docs.title: 4a. Load the Robot Configuration
docs.text:
You have two options to provide the JSON file:

Paste the PathBrowse for the File
  1. Click in the text field that appears in the game view
  2. Paste the file path (Cmd+V) — the one you copied with Option+Cmd+C in the previous step
  3. Press Enter
  1. Click the "Browse…" button in the game view
  2. Navigate to your robot_config.json file
  3. Select it and confirm

docs.title: 4b. Enter the MQTT Broker Address
docs.text:
Fill in the MQTT broker address field using the format:

address:port

For a broker running locally on your Mac:

127.0.0.1:1883

The default Mosquitto port is 1883

If you haven't changed the Mosquitto configuration, use 127.0.0.1:1883.

docs.title: 4c. Start the Simulation
docs.text: Click the Start button (or equivalent) in the game UI. The robots should appear at their configured positions in the arena.

docs.title: Step 5 — Navigate the View
docs.text: Once the simulation is running, use these controls to navigate the camera:

docs.title: Camera Controls
docs.text:
Action Keys Zoom in Up Zoom out Down Pan right Right Pan left Left Rotate view Shift+Up / Shift+Down / Shift+Left / Shift+Right

View Rotation — Work in Progress

The Shift + arrow key rotation controls are experimental and may behave unexpectedly. Stick to zoom and pan for now.

docs.title: Step 6 — Send MQTT Commands
docs.text: With the broker running and Unity connected, you can control robots by publishing MQTT messages from any terminal.

docs.title: Example Commands
docs.text:
# Send a velocity command to a robot
mosquitto_pub -h 127.0.0.1 -t "arena/sparknode01/cmd" \
  -m "drive forward 32 3000"

# Stop a specific robot
mosquitto_pub -h 127.0.0.1 -t "arena/sparknode01/cmd" \
  -m "stop"

# Monitor all MQTT traffic (useful for debugging)
mosquitto_sub -h 127.0.0.1 -t "#" -v

Unity Window Must Be Active

The Unity game window must be in focus (the active window) for robot movement to be visible. If robots aren't moving, click on the Unity Game view to bring it to the foreground.

docs.title: Summary: What Should Be Running
docs.text:
At this point you should have:

Terminal / App What's Running Status Terminal 1 mosquitto broker Running (keep open) Terminal 2 robot_traj_http.py Running (optional — only for physical robots) Terminal 3 Your working terminal For mosquitto_pub / mosquitto_sub commands Unity Editor SparkVerse simulation Playing

docs.title: Troubleshooting Quick Fixes
docs.text: Problem Fix Robots don't appear Check the JSON file path was entered correctly Robots don't move Make sure the Unity game window is active (in focus) "Connection refused" in Unity Verify the broker is running and the address is 127.0.0.1:1883 Camera script crashes Check Python dependencies are installed (pip3 install opencv-python numpy) Wrong camera selected Change the camera index in robot_traj_http.py (default is 0)

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Follow these three steps in order to get SparkVerse running on your Mac:

Step What Time 1 Unity Setup — Clone the repo, open the project in Unity Hub ~15 min 2 MQTT Broker — Install and configure Mosquitto via Homebrew ~5 min 3 Python Dependencies — Install packages for the camera detection script ~5 min

Platform

This guide is written for macOS on Apple Silicon (M1 / M2 / M3 / M4). The project has been tested on Unity 6.3 LTS and Mosquitto 2.1.2.

Using TurtleBots instead of SparkNodes?

If you're setting up the TurtleVerse variant (TurtleBot3 + Qualisys motion capture), head to the TurtleVerse Installation guide instead.

docs.title: MQTT Broker Setup
docs.text: SparkVerse uses MQTT as its communication backbone. All robot commands and pose data flow through a local Mosquitto broker running on your Mac.

docs.title: 1. Install Homebrew (if needed)
docs.text:
If you don't have Homebrew yet:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Verify the installation:

brew --version

docs.title: 2. Install Mosquitto
docs.text:
brew install mosquitto

This installs Mosquitto v2.1.2 (or latest). Verify:

mosquitto -h 2>&1 | head -1

You should see something like:

mosquitto version 2.1.2

docs.title: 3. Start the Broker
docs.text:
Open a dedicated terminal window and start the broker:

/opt/homebrew/opt/mosquitto/sbin/mosquitto -c /opt/homebrew/etc/mosquitto/mosquitto.conf

You should see:

1713437136: mosquitto version 2.1.2 starting
1713437136: Config loaded from /opt/homebrew/etc/mosquitto/mosquitto.conf
1713437136: Opening ipv4 listen socket on port 1883.
1713437136: mosquitto version 2.1.2 running

Keep This Terminal Open

The broker runs in the foreground. Do not close this terminal while using SparkVerse. Open new terminal tabs/windows for other commands.

docs.title: 4. Verify the Broker Is Working
docs.text:
Open two new terminal windows and test the pub/sub flow:

Terminal A — SubscribeTerminal B — Publish 
mosquitto_sub -h 127.0.0.1 -t "test/#"

mosquitto_pub -h 127.0.0.1 -t "test/ping" -m "hello from mosquitto"

You should see hello from mosquitto appear in Terminal A.

Broker is ready

If you see the message, your MQTT broker is working correctly. You can close Terminal A and B — they were just for verification.

docs.title: Alternative: Run as a Background Service
docs.text:
If you prefer the broker to run automatically in the background:

brew services start mosquitto

To stop it later:

brew services stop mosquitto

To check if it's running:

brew services list | grep mosquitto

Foreground vs Background

Running in the foreground (the method in Step 3) is recommended during development because you can see connection logs in real-time. Use the background service for convenience once everything is stable.

docs.title: Mosquitto Clients (Optional but Helpful)
docs.text:
The mosquitto_sub and mosquitto_pub command-line tools are installed alongside the broker. They are invaluable for debugging:

# Monitor ALL MQTT traffic (very useful for debugging)
mosquitto_sub -h 127.0.0.1 -t "#" -v

# Send a test command to a specific robot
mosquitto_pub -h 127.0.0.1 -t "arena/sparknode07/cmd" -m "stop"

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text: Continue to Python Dependencies to set up the camera detection script.

docs.title: Python Dependencies
docs.text: The camera-based robot detection script (robot_traj_http.py) requires several Python packages. This page walks through installing them.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure you have Python 3 installed (macOS ships with Python 3 on recent versions):

python3 --version

You should see Python 3.10 or higher.

docs.title: Install Dependencies
docs.text:
Install all required packages in a single command:

pip3 install opencv-python numpy

docs.title: Package Breakdown
docs.text:
Package Version Purpose opencv-python ≥ 4.5 Camera capture, image processing, circle/ArUco detection numpy ≥ 1.21 Array operations, Kalman filter matrices

These are the only external packages needed. The remaining imports used by robot_traj_http.py are all part of the Python standard library:

Standard Library Module Purpose cv2 Installed via opencv-python above numpy Installed above time, sys, math Timing, system, trigonometry csv, os, json File I/O and config parsing threading Background HTTP server thread http.server Built-in HTTP server for Unity data collections.deque Sliding window for pose smoothing

Local Module: database.py

The script imports database, which is a local module included in the MAPF_sparkbug repository alongside robot_traj_http.py. No separate installation is needed — just run the script from the MAPF_sparkbug/ directory so Python can find it.

database.py is a De Bruijn sequence codebook used for robot identification. Each SparkNode has a ring of 16 RGB LEDs on top, and each robot is assigned a unique 16-element colour sequence (Cyan / Magenta / Yellow / Green). The overhead camera reads this LED pattern to identify which robot is which — even if robots move or rotate — by matching the observed pattern against the codebook.

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
Run a quick check to make sure everything is importable:

python3 -c "import cv2; import numpy; print(f'OpenCV {cv2.__version__}, NumPy {numpy.__version__}')"

Expected output:

OpenCV 4.11.0, NumPy 2.2.6

(Exact version numbers may differ — that's fine.)

docs.title: Camera Access
docs.text:
The detection script uses your Mac's camera. On first run, macOS will prompt for camera access — make sure to Allow it.

To list available cameras:

ffmpeg -f avfoundation -list_devices true -i "" 2>&1 | grep "video"

Camera Index

By default, camera index 0 is the built-in FaceTime camera. If using an external camera (e.g. iPhone via Continuity Camera), it will typically be index 1 or 2. You can change this in the script.

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text: All dependencies are installed. Continue to Running the Simulation to launch everything.

docs.title: 1. Install Unity Hub
docs.text:
If you don't already have Unity Hub installed:

  1. Download Unity Hub from unity.com/download
  2. Install and open Unity Hub
  3. Sign in with your Unity account (a free Personal licence is fine)

docs.title: 2. Install the Correct Unity Version
docs.text:
SparkVerse requires Unity 6.3 LTS (version 6000.3.2f1).

In Unity Hub:

  1. Go to Installs → Install Editor
  2. Select Unity 6.3 LTS (6000.3.2f1)
  3. Under modules, ensure at minimum:
    • Mac Build Support is checked
  4. Click Install and wait for the download to complete

Version Matters

The project has been built and tested on 6000.3.2f1. Using a different major version may cause shader, prefab, or API compatibility issues. Always use this exact version.

docs.title: 3. Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Open a terminal and clone the SparkVerse Unity project:

git clone https://github.com/vedantA04/sparkverse.git

This repository includes everything you need:

What's Included Description Prefabs Pre-configured robot models for the arena C# Scripts All game logic — robot spawning, MQTT handling, camera control M2MQTT Library The MQTT client library for Unity (already integrated, no separate install needed) Scene Files The main simulation scene, ready to run

docs.title: 4. Open the Project in Unity Hub
docs.text:
1. In Unity Hub, click Projects → Open (or Add)
  2. Navigate to the cloned sparkverse folder and select it
  3. Unity Hub will detect the project and associate it with Unity 6000.3.2f1
  4. Click to open — the first import may take a few minutes as Unity compiles shaders and imports assets

First Launch

The initial open will show a progress bar as Unity imports all assets and recompiles scripts. This is normal and can take 3–5 minutes depending on your machine. Subsequent opens will be much faster.

docs.title: 5. Verify the Project
docs.text:
Once the editor finishes loading:

  1. In the Project panel, you should see folders for Scripts, Prefabs, Scenes, etc.

  2. The project contains two scenes:

    Scene Purpose Start Scene Entry point — handles configuration loading (JSON file, MQTT address) Simulation Scene The main arena with robot spawning, camera, and MQTT control

  3. You should see the arena floor and camera setup in the Scene view

docs.title: Set the Start Scene as the First Scene
docs.text:
The simulation must be launched from the Start Scene. You can either:

Set it in Build Settings (Recommended)Run Manually Each Time
  1. Go to File → Build Settings (Cmd+Shift+B)
  2. Drag the Start Scene to the top of the Scenes in Build list (index 0)
  3. Drag the Simulation Scene below it (index 1)
  4. Close Build Settings

Now pressing Play from the Start Scene will flow correctly into the Simulation Scene.

  1. In the Project panel, navigate to Assets/Scenes/
  2. Double-click the Start Scene to open it
  3. Press Play (▶)

The Start Scene will load the configuration and transition to the Simulation Scene automatically.

Don't start from the Simulation Scene directly

If you press Play while the Simulation Scene is open, the configuration step will be skipped and robots won't spawn correctly. Always start from the Start Scene.

No Errors?

Check the Console panel (Cmd+Shift+C) — there should be no red errors. Yellow warnings about deprecated APIs are generally safe to ignore.

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text: The Unity project is ready, but it needs an MQTT broker to communicate. Continue to MQTT Broker Setup.

docs.title: TurtleVerse
docs.text:
TurtleVerse is the TurtleBot3 variant of the SparkVerse hybrid HIL platform. Instead of SparkNodes tracked by an overhead camera (as in the Monash campus setup), TurtleVerse uses TurtleBot3 Burger differential-drive robots localised by a Qualisys motion capture system.

The core architecture remains the same — MQTT as the communication backbone, Unity as the visualisation and digital-twin engine — but the perception and actuation layers are swapped:

SparkVerse (Monash) TurtleVerse (IIT Bombay) Robots SparkNodes (custom 2WD) TurtleBot3 Burger (ROS2) Localisation Overhead camera + OpenCV Qualisys motion capture (6-DOF) Robot control Direct MQTT → SparkNode firmware MQTT → ROS2 bridge → TurtleBot3 Location Monash University, Australia IIT Bombay, India

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The system forms a closed Hardware-in-the-Loop control cycle running at 20 Hz. All subsystems communicate through a central MQTT broker on the Mac.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Physical["Physical Space"]
        QTM["Qualisys MoCap"]
        TB["TurtleBot3 Burgers"]
    end

    subgraph Mac["MacBook (Central Hub)"]
        QTM_PY["run_qtm.py"]
        BROKER["Mosquitto MQTT Broker"]
        BRIDGE["mac_fleet_bridge.py\n(ROS2 ↔ MQTT)"]
        CMD["SwarmCommander.py"]
    end

    subgraph Unity["Unity Digital Twin"]
        TRACKER["RealRobotTracker.cs"]
        SIM["SimulatedBurger.cs"]
    end

    QTM -- "6-DOF rigid bodies" --> QTM_PY
    QTM_PY -- "turtle_verse/robotN/pose" --> BROKER
    BROKER -- "poses" --> CMD
    CMD -- "turtle_verse/robotN/cmd_vel" --> BROKER
    BROKER -- "cmd_vel" --> BRIDGE
    BRIDGE -- "ROS2 /robotN/cmd_vel" --> TB
    BROKER -- "poses" --> TRACKER
    BROKER -- "cmd_vel" --> SIM
    SIM -- "turtle_verse/simulatedN/pose" --> BROKER

docs.title: MQTT Topic Tree
docs.text:
All TurtleVerse topics live under the turtle_verse/ namespace:

turtle_verse/
├── robot1/
│   ├── pose              # Published by run_qtm.py (from Qualisys)
│   └── cmd_vel           # Published by SwarmCommander.py
├── robot2/
│   ├── pose
│   └── cmd_vel
├── robot3/
│   ├── pose
│   └── cmd_vel
├── simulated1/
│   ├── pose              # Published by SimulatedBurger.cs (from Unity)
│   └── cmd_vel           # Consumed by SimulatedBurger.cs
├── simulated2/
│   ├── pose
│   └── cmd_vel
└── fleet/
    └── system            # E-STOP / PAUSE (global)

docs.title: Payload Formats
docs.text:
Pose (turtle_verse/{name}/pose):

{"x": 1.2345, "y": 0.6789, "theta": 1.5708}

All values are in metres and radians (right-handed Cartesian).

Command Velocity (turtle_verse/{name}/cmd_vel):

{"linear": 0.12, "angular": 0.3}

Linear velocity in m/s, angular velocity in rad/s. Clamped to TurtleBot3 Burger hardware limits: ±0.22 m/s linear, ±2.84 rad/s angular.

docs.title: Components at a Glance
docs.text: Component Language Role run_qtm.py Python Streams Qualisys MoCap poses to MQTT mac_fleet_bridge.py Python (ROS2) Bridges MQTT velocity commands to ROS2 /cmd_vel topics SwarmCommander.py Python Central swarm controller (cyclic pursuit / leader-follower) commander_square.py Python Same controller with leader-follower square defaults RealRobotTracker.cs C# (Unity) Mirrors physical robot poses inside Unity SimulatedBurger.cs C# (Unity) Fully simulated digital-twin robot in Unity MqttPayloads.cs C# (Unity) Shared serialisable data classes for MQTT JSON

docs.title: Future Scope
docs.text:
SparkVerse currently operates in two standalone configurations:

  • SparkNodes tracked by an overhead camera at Monash University, Australia
  • TurtleBot3 Burgers tracked by Qualisys MoCap at IIT Bombay, India

Both variants share the same MQTT-based architecture and Unity digital-twin engine. The natural next step is to combine them.

docs.title: Heterogeneous Multi-Site Simulation
docs.text:
The long-term vision is a heterogeneous swarm operating across multiple geographic locations within a single unified simulation:

flowchart TB
    subgraph IITBombay["IIT Bombay, India"]
        TB3["TurtleBot3 Burgers"]
        QTM["Qualisys MoCap"]
    end

    subgraph Monash["Monash University, Australia"]
        SN["SparkNodes"]
        CAM["Overhead Camera"]
    end

    subgraph Cloud["Unified Simulation"]
        UNITY["Unity Digital Twin"]
        DIGITAL["Fully Digital 2WD Robots"]
    end

    TB3 --> UNITY
    QTM --> UNITY
    SN --> UNITY
    CAM --> UNITY
    DIGITAL --> UNITY

In this setup:

  • Physical TurtleBots in India contribute their Qualisys-tracked poses to the shared simulation
  • Physical SparkNodes in Australia contribute their camera-tracked poses
  • Fully digital 2WD robots exist only inside Unity with no physical counterpart
  • A single swarm commander orchestrates all agents — physical and virtual, local and remote — as one unified fleet

docs.title: TurtleVerse Installation
docs.text:
This page covers everything you need to install before running TurtleVerse. The setup consists of four parts:

Step What Time 1 Unity Project — Clone the TurtleVerse Unity project ~15 min 2 MQTT Broker — Same Mosquitto setup as SparkVerse ~5 min 3 Qualisys Python Bridge — Install dependencies for run_qtm.py ~5 min 4 ROS2 Humble (RoboStack) — Required for mac_fleet_bridge.py ~15 min 5 Swarm Commander Dependencies — Python packages for the control scripts ~2 min

Platform

This guide is written for macOS on Apple Silicon (M1 / M2 / M3 / M4). The TurtleBots run ROS2 Humble on their onboard Raspberry Pi.

docs.title: 1. Unity Project
docs.text:
The TurtleVerse Unity project is separate from the SparkVerse Unity project. It contains the TurtleBot3-specific prefabs, scenes, and C# scripts (RealRobotTracker.cs, SimulatedBurger.cs, MqttPayloads.cs).

Repository — Coming Soon

The TurtleVerse Unity project GitHub repository is not yet public. This section will be updated with the clone URL once it is available.

Once the repository is available:

  1. Install Unity Hub and Unity 6.3 LTS (6000.3.2f1) — same version as SparkVerse. See the SparkVerse Unity Setup for detailed steps.
  2. Clone the TurtleVerse repository.
  3. Open the project in Unity Hub.

docs.title: 2. MQTT Broker
docs.text:
TurtleVerse uses the same Mosquitto MQTT broker as SparkVerse. If you've already set it up, you're good to go.

If not, follow the MQTT Broker Setup guide.

docs.title: 3. Qualisys Python Bridge
docs.text: The run_qtm.py script connects to the Qualisys Track Manager (QTM) software over the network, reads 6-DOF rigid body data, and publishes standardised poses to MQTT.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
pip3 install qtm-rt paho-mqtt
Package Purpose qtm-rt Async Python SDK for the Qualisys Real-Time protocol paho-mqtt MQTT client library for publishing poses to the broker

Standard library modules used: asyncio, json, math.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
python3 -c "import qtm_rt; import paho.mqtt.client; print('Qualisys bridge deps OK')"

Network Requirement

Your Mac must be on the same Wi-Fi network as the Qualisys MoCap PC. The default QTM IP in the script is 192.168.0.126 — update this to match your Qualisys PC's address.

docs.title: 4. ROS2 Humble via RoboStack
docs.text:
The mac_fleet_bridge.py script is a ROS2 node that subscribes to MQTT velocity commands and republishes them as ROS2 geometry_msgs/Twist messages for the TurtleBots. This requires a working ROS2 Humble installation on your Mac.

The recommended approach for macOS is RoboStack — a conda-based distribution of ROS2. Follow the RoboStack installation guide to set up a ROS2 Humble conda environment on your Mac.

ROS_DOMAIN_ID

All devices (Mac and TurtleBots) must share the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID. Set it in every terminal before running ROS2 commands:

export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=<your_domain_id>

Replace <your_domain_id> with the ID your TurtleBots are configured to use.

docs.title: Dependencies for mac_fleet_bridge.py
docs.text: Package Source Purpose rclpy ROS2 Humble (via RoboStack) ROS2 Python client library geometry_msgs ROS2 Humble (via RoboStack) Twist message type for velocity commands paho-mqtt pip MQTT client for receiving commands from the broker

docs.title: TurtleBot3 Side Setup
docs.text:
TurtleBot3 Preparation

Each TurtleBot3 Burger runs ROS2 Humble on a Raspberry Pi. Before TurtleVerse can control them, the TurtleBots must be running their ROS2 bringup nodes.

SSH into each TurtleBot and run:

ssh ubuntu@<turtlebot_ip>
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=<your_domain_id>
ros2 launch turtlebot3_bringup robot.launch.py

This starts the motor controller and cmd_vel subscriber on the TurtleBot.

To verify from your Mac (with the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID):

ros2 topic list

You should see topics like /robot1/cmd_vel, etc.

Auto-Bringup on Boot

You can configure each TurtleBot's Raspberry Pi to automatically run the bringup launch file on boot (e.g., via a systemd service). This way, you only need to power on the robots and ensure they connect to the same Wi-Fi — no SSH required during normal operation. All you need on your Mac is:

export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=<your_domain_id>

docs.title: 5. Swarm Commander Dependencies
docs.text:
Both SwarmCommander.py and commander_square.py (which share the same codebase with different default configurations) require only:

pip3 install paho-mqtt
Package Purpose paho-mqtt MQTT client for subscribing to poses and publishing velocity commands

Standard library modules used: json, time, math.

docs.title: Dependencies Summary
docs.text: Script Python Packages System Requirements run_qtm.py qtm-rt, paho-mqtt Same Wi-Fi as Qualisys PC mac_fleet_bridge.py paho-mqtt, rclpy, geometry_msgs ROS2 Humble (RoboStack) SwarmCommander.py paho-mqtt — commander_square.py paho-mqtt —

docs.title: What's Next
docs.text: All dependencies are installed. Continue to Running TurtleVerse to launch everything.

docs.title: Running TurtleVerse
docs.text: This guide assumes you've completed all installation steps. You'll need four or more terminal windows plus the Unity editor.

docs.title: Step 1 — Start the MQTT Broker
docs.text:
Open a terminal and start Mosquitto:

/opt/homebrew/opt/mosquitto/sbin/mosquitto -c /opt/homebrew/etc/mosquitto/mosquitto.conf

Or, if you set it up as a background service:

brew services start mosquitto

Keep the broker running

The MQTT broker must stay running for the entire session. Every component — Qualisys bridge, Unity, fleet bridge, commander — communicates through it.

docs.title: Step 2 — Connect to the Qualisys Network
docs.text:
Ensure your Mac is on the same Wi-Fi network as the Qualisys MoCap PC. The QTM software must be running on the MoCap PC with the rigid bodies (TurtleBots) defined and streaming.

QTM IP Address

The default IP in run_qtm.py is 192.168.0.126. If your Qualisys PC has a different IP, update the QTM_PC_IP variable in the script before running.

docs.title: Step 3 — Stream Qualisys Poses
docs.text:
Open a new terminal and run the Qualisys-to-MQTT bridge:

python3 run_qtm.py

You should see output like:

MQTT Connected!
Bridging Standardized Poses to MQTT (Meters & Radians)...

Published -> turtle_verse/robot1/pose : {'x': 1.2345, 'y': 0.6789, 'theta': 1.5708}
Published -> turtle_verse/robot2/pose : {'x': 0.8012, 'y': 1.3456, 'theta': -0.7854}
...

This script continuously reads 6-DOF rigid body data from QTM, converts positions from millimetres to metres, extracts yaw from the rotation matrix, and publishes to turtle_verse/robotN/pose.

docs.title: Step 4 — Start the ROS2 Fleet Bridge
docs.text:
Open a new terminal, activate your ROS2 environment, and run the bridge:

conda activate ros2humble
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=<your_domain_id>
python3 mac_fleet_bridge.py

You should see:

Connecting to MQTT broker at 127.0.0.1...
Connected to Broker! Listening to ALL robots on: turtle_verse/+/cmd_vel

Keep this running in the background

The fleet bridge must stay running. It subscribes to MQTT velocity commands (turtle_verse/{robot}/cmd_vel) and dynamically creates ROS2 publishers for each robot it discovers. When a new robot name appears in the MQTT topics, it automatically creates a /robot_name/cmd_vel ROS2 publisher.

TurtleBots Must Be Running

Make sure each TurtleBot3 is powered on and running its ROS2 bringup (either via SSH or auto-boot). They must be on the same Wi-Fi and the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID.

docs.title: Step 5 — Launch Unity
docs.text:
1. Open the TurtleVerse Unity project in Unity Hub.
  2. Open the main scene.
  3. Press Play (▶).

Unity will connect to the MQTT broker and:

  • RealRobotTracker objects will mirror the physical TurtleBot poses from Qualisys.
  • SimulatedBurger objects will listen for cmd_vel commands and simulate digital-twin robots.

Unity MQTT Configuration

Each robot GameObject in the Unity scene has a brokerIP field in the Inspector. Set this to 127.0.0.1 if the broker is running locally on your Mac.

docs.title: Step 6 — Run a Swarm Commander
docs.text:
Open a new terminal and launch one of the swarm control scripts:

Leader-Follower (Square Waypoints)Cyclic Pursuit 
python3 commander_square.py

The leader (robot1) follows a square path through predefined waypoints. All other robots in the chain follow in sequence using pure pursuit.

python3 SwarmCommander.py

All robots form a closed pursuit ring — each agent chases the next in a circular topology.

Both scripts include a 5-second safety countdown before engaging the swarm:

Swarm engaging in 5 seconds... (Press Ctrl+C to abort)
Swarm engaging in 4 seconds... (Press Ctrl+C to abort)
...
🚀 GO! 🚀

Safety

Always be ready to press Ctrl+C to stop the commander. This sends zero-velocity commands to all robots before shutting down.

docs.title: Summary: What Should Be Running
docs.text: Terminal / App What's Running Status Terminal 1 mosquitto broker Running (keep open) Terminal 2 run_qtm.py (Qualisys → MQTT) Streaming poses Terminal 3 mac_fleet_bridge.py (MQTT → ROS2) Bridging commands Terminal 4 SwarmCommander.py or commander_square.py Controlling swarm Unity Editor TurtleVerse simulation Playing

docs.title: Troubleshooting Quick Fixes
docs.text: Problem Fix run_qtm.py won't connect Verify Mac is on the same Wi-Fi as the Qualisys PC; check QTM_PC_IP No pose data in Unity Verify run_qtm.py is printing poses; check MQTT with mosquitto_sub -h 127.0.0.1 -t "turtle_verse/#" -v TurtleBots don't move Check mac_fleet_bridge.py is running; verify ROS_DOMAIN_ID matches; confirm TurtleBot bringup is active Unity robots jitter This is normal at high update rates — RealRobotTracker applies Lerp smoothing. Ensure QTM is tracking markers cleanly "Connection refused" Make sure the MQTT broker is running on port 1883 Commander crashes immediately Ensure paho-mqtt is installed (pip3 install paho-mqtt)
